content:

title: Ausangate
excerpt: Notes from the trail around Peru's rainbow mountain.
content:
First of all I would like to state here that this was the **hardest hike I have done so far in my life**, but also the coolest. As soon as I came back from Peru and people figured out I went to Cusco, absolutely everyone asked me the question **~how was macchu picchu???~** To be honest, every time I heard that question I got hurt, as if I was a nail and the question was like a huge hammer coming to stamp one single label onto a whole vast and diverse culture. Peru is simply amazing: the people, the landscapes, the food and any other subject you can imagine. When in Cusco, since I didn't plan anything beforehand, I needed to make a decision: **Machu Picchu or Ausangate**. Well, if you have a decent amount of neurons you know my decision. 

 After making my decision for Ausangate I started to stress the internet and travel agencies (which I'm most of the time against) looking for something affordable. It was impossible. Based on the challenge level of the hike, the number of days (4 to 5) and the equipment, the prices are basically InSaNe! Luckily I found somewhere the number of a local guide who actually lives together with his whole family creright there! Cirilo is his name! After a few messages he told me he would be around Cusco the next day and we agreed to talk. The price was fair: 900 soles. Basically 25% of the cheapest price I had found so far, and all included (tent, food, water). Besides, all the money stays with the community in Ausangate - **no middle man!** Ahh, one important detail: since I was alone, I was also looking for a group to join, since private guidance was out of the question. Cirilo told me there were two italian dudes that maybe wouldn't mind if I joined, and they didn't in the end. The Francescos! Both from Milan. I can say we are good friends now, and the craziest thing is that both could speak portuguese since they learned it in their capoeira practices. 

 After settling the deal I departed the next morning together with the Francescos and 3 other people from Belgium who would split off to go to the rainbow mountains on the second day. We drove a long way to Tinki and from there up to the starting point: Cirilo's house! His wife received us with a simple but nice breakfast. From there we hiked to Tinki, all the way facing the crazy mountains that were getting closer and closer. The terrain was humid and unique, high altitude, flat and hilly, green with some water spots and so many alpacas. The day was beautiful when we reached Upis, where we stayed for the night. The belgians split off at the beginning since they were doing only 2 or 3 days and finishing halfway, at the rainbow mountains. So they were at the 7 lakes in the morning and we met in Upis in the afternoon. The second day we started the hike passing through paso de arapa and paso de apacheta, and finally we split, I guess in ananta. All the way such a beautiful rocky terrain, with some interesting weird fauna and flora, and hot springs. Pumacocha lake from a top perspective while taking a break is something I will never forget. Me and the Francescos kept hiking and we passed through the paradiseish ausangate pass and its stunning ausangate lake. This was one of the most beautiful days of my life, like something I had never seen before, in perfect weather. 

 We rested at a camp site at the beginning of the route to palomani pass. It rained that night quite a lot. I was told Palomani pass is the highest pass of the trail, so I started to use as much coca leaf as possible the day before already, in all possible ways (tea, candy, leaves both chewing and leaving them in the gum). This desperate action was due to the hard altitude hit I got on the first day. Luckily the belgian crew was composed of two doctors holding ibuprofen and other drugs for altitude, which they kindly gave to me. I slept like a baby after that. Anyways, that night I was very focused on resting for the highest pass the next day, which was around 5.2 thousand meters! 

 I confess I was afraid that day but of course, as a regular average everyday man, I didn't share it with anybody. The route was very steep from the beginning. It was really hard but gorgeous. When we finally reached the pass I almost cried - **the highest place I have been in my entire life**, and it was beautiful. It looked exactly like the rainbow mountain and all its layers, but with no one there. We chilled there and everyone was happy. Here are the photos with the Francescos and the two from the crew (the guide and the caballero). 

 ![With the Francescos and the crew at the highest pass](/images/ausangate_crew.jpeg#65%) 

 The horses were amazing tho, incredible endurance for the mountains, probably a breed that adapted to the altitude, which maybe could be the reason why they were quite small. We walked all the way around the back of the Ausangate mountain that day, incredible landscape and a huge contrast between the deep dark rocks, blue lake, white snow and rainbow colors on the opposite side. We hiked a lot that day, like a lot. **The toughest day for sure.** After the pass you go flat, then down like a valley, and then you need to go all the way up again, passing 5000 meters at jampa pass. Massive effort but we all did it, with a few breaks and even a 15 min nap during the route. However, the weather got us as soon as we got to the highest spot. I can't even describe what actually happened. Insane wind, ice and snow at the same time. I have been in snowstorms before but nothing like that. It was snow, ice, harsh wind and fog at the same time. I couldn't see even 5 meters in front of me. We proceeded carefully and we didn't dare to stay there to see one of the iconic views from the path, a lagoon view between the red mountains that I can't even remember because of the fear at that point. Unfortunately we missed that for the sake of safety. Having overcome that weather, we started descending to the last camp site, almost inside the west part of the Ausangate mountain, with some ancient buildings from a previous village, I assume. From there the sky at night was so pretty and all around us were incredible mountains. It looked as if we were being wrapped by it when spinning the eyes around the tents. 

 Last day up we honestly just enjoyed it since the hardest part was behind us. 7 lakes, that's how they call them. It is so pretty but also very touristic. We were lucky we were there very early morning since we camped there, and it was so funny to see the people coming while we were returning. Once we reached the last spot of the hike we just chilled and ate something. We also played some chess and I beat both Italians more than once, probably out of pure luck. The crew were amazing and very friendly. I hope they are well. They told us that they work on the trail almost every week with two or three days of resting between each new start. Crazy and tough life but also simply beautiful. I wonder how many times they have surrounded that mountain already. I headed back to Tinki after a few hours and then we got an intercity public bus back to Cusco. Sad and happy that it was over, hard to explain. I hope I never forget those memories. This is what I got from Ausangate: beautiful memories filled with landscapes, alpacas, aquaflorida and coca, respect for the mountains and two random italian friends that speak portuguese and practice capoeira. 

 ![Coca leaves and agua florida](/images/ausangate_coca_and_aquaflorida.jpeg#65%) 

 If you are reading this, thank you guys for the fellowship, the jokes around and for sharing your coca leaves. Hear me out, I still want to go one day to Macchu Picchu and it is probably incredible but I think choosing Ausangate this time was **my best trip decision**. Maybe even of all the trips I have done until now. 

 I extremely recommend Cirilo and his crew as a guide for Ausangate. Here is his phone/whatsapp: +51 941 005 350

title: A Maybe Stability Letter for Life's Vagrants
excerpt: Does a stable life really exist, or is it just a myth?
content:
Over the last few days I have been thinking a lot about what a stable life is. Does it really exist, or is it just a myth? Well, approaching this question as an engineer, my first instinct is to think about entropy. The second law of thermodynamics states that the entropy of an isolated system can never decrease. It can only increase or, at best, stay the same. Therefore, can we say that if we achieve zero entropy, the system is stable? Probably yes, but then nothing happens. Life is action and randomness. So what is the point of seeking stability? Maybe to have the illusion of peace and to accomplish things without putting in extra effort. Perhaps it is also some kind of automation applied to day-to-day life, such as routines and scheduled activities. From my perspective, this is even sadder than having no control over your life at all.

I would be lying if I said I don't like having some kind of routine. I'm human after all (I think), and to some degree I like having an "expectation" of what will happen tomorrow, next week or next month. Why do we need this to feel at peace? This urge might come from many thousands of years ago, when we stopped being hunter-gatherers and started worrying about the next harvest or whether a wolf had killed half of the flock. Were our prehistoric ancestors less stressed than humans in today's modern society? Hard to say, since lives back then were much shorter and surviving took a huge hustle. Besides, nobody from that period knew what Google Meet or Microsoft Teams were, and they are all resting in peace (deceased) anyway.

There is no way I leave home without taking my creatine and marking an X on the calendar hanging from a single screw on the electrical panel in my kitchen. The body absorbs creatine much better when you take it together with carbs, which goes pretty well with oats or bread in the morning. However, it has been a few months now since I stopped eating breakfast. Why do I still take creatine in the morning, then? Because it brings me comfort, and I don't know why. Maybe that's why I'm writing about this.

Comfort is also what many people look for in their careers. The search for a stable job is still present in my generation (based on my bubble), but much less than in my parents' generation. My mom used to say "se tu trabalhar concursado ou para uma multinacional tu estará com a vida feita", which means that if you work in the public sector or for a multinational company, you will have everything you need for a good life, which can also be understood as a stable life. Let's look at the two options in that statement. Now imagine yourself working for a big tech company. There have been many examples of huge layoffs in recent years, so we can be certain it doesn't mean stability, even if you deliver your best and are the best at what you do. That's because, ultimately, a job is also politics and internal/external networking. Human relations sometimes affect your job more than your actual work does, even in an extremely technical position. Times have changed, and the peaceful period the world had after WWII and the Cold War seems to be over, unfortunately, which also affects multinational companies.

I have to agree with my mom, Nina, that working in the public sector is not bad at all. And yes, depending on the country, it is basically impossible to get fired if you do the bare minimum of the minimum of the minimum... (10x). I can say that about Brazil, and probably other places as well. There you would be able to achieve "work stability", but isn't that super boring? What motivation do you have to wake up and go to work if you know that most people will be doing the minimum? What can you accomplish in life working in a place like that? You would certainly have much less stress than working for a private company, but then what is the meaning behind it? There is no right or wrong, just people who think differently.

I live in an endless contrast between where I'm from and where I live now. In Denmark, if you want to do something (even with your friends!), you need to book it and ask them to block their calendars. I still can't fully adapt to it, even though I consider myself someone who adapts quite fast to different environments. Anyway, I guess that's because it is not only boring but also takes away a bit of the magic of life. Spontaneity, surprise, and fortuitous chance should be the natural way things happen, accepting positive entropy and handling it. In Brazil we might even have too much of it, and that could be why Brazilians are well known for being so good at handling uncertainty and pressure. What an antithesis: born and raised in Brazil, living in Denmark.

Nothing to complain about, though, since I'm living a good life here, in a country my dad never visited even though he lived in Europe for many years. I imagine that in his time the land of Søren Kierkegaard, Niels Bohr, The Little Mermaid and The Ugly Duckling (Hans Christian Andersen), Brøndby IF, Lego, Maersk, Novo Nordisk, Vestas, Ørestad, Carlsberg, Danfoss, DSV and many others was not as fancy and stylish as it is today. I can't judge him, since he was living in Paris in its prime! But my dad's crazy stories are a topic for another day. Notice how many of the names I just mentioned are multinational companies that started in Denmark. Is that an indication that it is a stable country?

There is a scent in the air in Europe that you start noticing after a few years of living here. It is a weird feeling of constant instability, as if something could be disrupted at any moment. Have you heard of the Heartland and Rimland theories? I'm confident they are at least partially true, and that whoever controls the Eurasian bloc also leads and orchestrates the world.

I have been reading a book of my dad's that I brought back the last time I went home and visited my stepmother, who has most of his collection since he passed away. It is a book about Pablo Neruda's life, written by himself. Wild stories, an old-school lifestyle and mentality, and shocking confessions make it a true masterpiece with nothing to hide. Maybe, being a wonderful poet, he softened a few passages or facts, but it is all still there. In one of the paragraphs of the short section called Winnipeg (the ship, organized by Neruda, that sailed from France to Chile to rescue Spanish refugees who had fled the Spanish Civil War after Francisco Franco's coup), there is a phrase that explains this feeling I share with the famous poet:

> Acostumei-me, naqueles dias crepusculares, a essa incerteza européia que não sofre revoluções contínuas nem terremotos mas mantém o veneno mortal da guerra saturando o ar e o pão.
> In those twilight days, I became accustomed to that European uncertainty which does not suffer continuous revolutions or earthquakes, but keeps the deadly poison of war saturating the air and the bread.
> -- Pablo Neruda, Confesso que Vivi

I wouldn't dare say we share the same context, because the times I live in are easier than the ones he went through, but the feeling is somehow similar. What I do dare say is that there will never be stability in Europe. Not in Europe, nor anywhere else on our tiny planet, with its 40,000 kilometers of circumference and 15 billion hectares of land.

I have no conclusion or answer, but that was never what I was aiming for when writing this. It is really hard to reflect on life in general. At the end of the day, we are all filled with different beliefs that make you and me who we are, and this difference in being can only increase entropy, making the world less and less stable. Extremism will never be the solution, under any circumstances. So could we say that stability is a continuous and steady increase of entropy, avoiding intense peaks? Does that make me conservative, since I'm basically advocating for progress in small, well-controlled steps, and I agree with a few arguments from both the left and the right wing? Let's leave politics out of this. As for me, I will keep taking my creatine every morning and marking my X on the calendar, a tiny dose of stability in a world of ever-increasing entropy. Hopefully, we're gonna find our way through life on board our own Winnipegs. A life with purpose might be the answer. But not everyone can find it. I truly hope you can spot it on your way.

Eduardo.
